questions.q: The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution of India on:
questions.src: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950.

questions.q: Among the historical precursors to the Indian Constitution, the single most significant structural template was:
questions.src: The Government of India Act 1935 provided the primary structural template (federal scheme, lists, judiciary structure) adapted by the Constituent Assembly.

questions.q: The Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly was chaired by:
questions.src: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee responsible for preparing the Constitution's text.

questions.q: Article 1 of the Constitution describes India as:
questions.src: Article 1 deliberately uses "Union of States" (not Federation), emphasising the indestructibility of the Union.

questions.q: The words "Socialist" and "Secular" were inserted into the Preamble by which amendment?
questions.src: The 42nd Amendment 1976 added "Socialist" and "Secular" to the Preamble.

questions.q: Under Article 13, a law made by the State that takes away or abridges Fundamental Rights is:
o: Valid if passed by a two-thirds majority
Void to the extent of such inconsistency
questions.src: Article 13(2) declares such a law void to the extent of the contravention.

questions.q: Under Article 12, the definition of "State" for Fundamental Rights purposes has been judicially extended to include:
o: Instrumentalities and agencies substantially controlled/financed by the government, alongside the government and local authorities
No bodies beyond the literal text at all
questions.src: Courts have extended "State" under Article 12 to cover government instrumentalities/agencies based on tests of substantial government control/financing.

questions.q: The test for a valid "reasonable classification" under Article 14 requires:
o: An intelligible differentia having a rational nexus to the object sought to be achieved
Classification is never permitted under Article 14
Classification based only on population size
questions.src: Article 14 permits reasonable classification if it satisfies both requirements: intelligible differentia AND rational nexus to the legislative object.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six freedoms guaranteed under Article 19(1) currently?
o: Freedom to acquire, hold, and dispose of property
Freedom to practise any profession, occupation, trade, or business
questions.src: The freedom to acquire/hold/dispose of property (originally 19(1)(f)) was removed by the 44th Amendment; property is now only a legal right under Article 300A, not a Fundamental Right.

questions.q: Article 20(2) of the Constitution protects against:
o: Double jeopardy — prosecution and punishment for the same offence more than once
questions.src: Article 20(2) specifically protects against double jeopardy.

questions.q: In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Supreme Court held that "procedure established by law" under Article 21 must be:
o: Any procedure enacted by a valid law, regardless of fairness
Applicable only to Indian citizens, never foreign nationals
questions.src: The Court held the procedure itself must be fair, just, and reasonable — not merely exist on paper — overruling the earlier narrow A.K. Gopalan interpretation.

questions.q: The "Golden Triangle" in Indian constitutional law, established in Maneka Gandhi, refers to the interlinked reading of:
questions.src: The Golden Triangle refers to Articles 14 (equality), 19 (freedoms), and 21 (life and liberty) being read together, not in isolation.

questions.q: Which earlier Supreme Court case did Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) overrule regarding Article 21?
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)
I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu
questions.src: Maneka Gandhi overruled the narrow interpretation of Article 21 established in A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950).

questions.q: Article 21-A, guaranteeing the Right to Education, was inserted by which constitutional amendment?
questions.src: The 86th Amendment 2002 inserted Article 21-A, guaranteeing free and compulsory education to children aged 6-14.

questions.q: Under Article 22, a person arrested must generally be produced before a magistrate within:
questions.src: Article 22(2) requires production before a magistrate within 24 hours of arrest, excluding the time necessary for the journey.

questions.q: Article 23 of the Constitution prohibits:
o: Traffic in human beings and begar (forced labour without payment)
questions.src: Article 23 specifically prohibits traffic in human beings and begar/other forms of forced labour.

questions.q: Article 25 protects the
o: Denomination's right to manage its own religious institutions
Individual's freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise, and propagate religion
Right to be free from all taxation
Right to establish educational institutions only
questions.src: Article 25 is the individual's right to freedom of conscience and religious profession/practice/propagation, distinguished from Article 26's institutional/denominational rights.

questions.q: Article 32, described by Dr. Ambedkar as the "heart and soul" of the Constitution, guarantees:
o: The right to move the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights
questions.src: Article 32 is the Right to Constitutional Remedies — direct access to the Supreme Court for enforcing Fundamental Rights via writs.

questions.q: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Supreme Court, sitting as a 13-judge bench, held that:
o: Parliament has completely unlimited power to amend any part of the Constitution
Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot destroy its "basic structure"
The Constitution can never be amended under any circumstances
Only the President can amend the Constitution
questions.src: The Basic Structure Doctrine established that Parliament's amending power under Article 368, while wide, cannot damage the Constitution's basic structure.

questions.q: The Kesavananda Bharati judgment was delivered on:
questions.src: The judgment was delivered on 24 April 1973, a date also significant as the cutoff for Ninth Schedule judicial review immunity established later in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu.

questions.q: Directive Principles of State Policy under Part IV of the Constitution are:
o: Directly enforceable in a court of law like Fundamental Rights
Non-justiciable, but fundamental in the governance of the country, guiding State policy-making
Applicable only during a state of emergency
questions.src: DPSPs are non-justiciable (not directly enforceable) but are fundamental guiding principles for governance and law-making.

questions.q: Article 44 of the Constitution, a Directive Principle, deals with:
questions.src: Article 44 directs the State to endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code for citizens throughout India, classified among the Liberal-Intellectual DPSPs.

questions.q: Fundamental Duties under Article 51-A were inserted into the Constitution by:
o: The 42nd Amendment 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee
questions.src: Article 51-A was added by the 42nd Amendment 1976, following the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation.

questions.q: Fundamental Duties under Article 51-A are:
o: Directly enforceable through a writ petition, exactly like Fundamental Rights
Morally significant but NOT directly enforceable through courts in the manner Fundamental Rights are
Identical in legal status to Directive Principles in every respect
questions.src: Fundamental Duties carry moral/civic significance but are not directly enforceable via courts the way Fundamental Rights (Part III) are.

questions.q: The relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, as increasingly recognised by courts, is best described as:
o: Total constitutional irrelevance of DPSPs to Fundamental Rights interpretation
Complementary — DPSPs are increasingly used as interpretive aids to expand the scope of certain Fundamental Rights, particularly Article 21
DPSPs always override Fundamental Rights automatically
Fundamental Rights were abolished in favour of DPSPs
questions.src: Courts have moved toward a harmonising approach, using DPSPs to inform and expand the interpretation of Fundamental Rights like Article 21, rather than treating them as entirely separate or subordinate.

questions.q: Under Article 19(2), restrictions on the freedom of speech and expression can be imposed only on:
o: Any ground the State considers fit, with no limitation

A closed, exhaustive list of specified grounds (sovereignty/integrity, security of State, public order, decency/morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to offence, friendly relations with foreign States)
Only grounds relating to national defence
No grounds whatsoever — the freedom is absolute
questions.src: Constitution of India, Article 19(2) — provides an exhaustive, closed list of permissible restriction grounds

questions.q: In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act primarily because it was:
o: Impermissibly vague and over-broad, creating a 'chilling effect' on legitimate speech without being narrowly tailored to any Article 19(2) ground
Not related to freedom of speech at all
questions.src: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (Supreme Court, 2015) — struck down Section 66A IT Act for vagueness/over-breadth and chilling effect on protected speech

questions.q: The Right to Property was removed from Part III (Fundamental Rights) of the Constitution and relocated to Article 300A by:
o: The original Constitution never included property as a Fundamental Right
questions.src: The 44th Amendment 1978 repealed Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31, inserting Article 300A in Part XII as a mere constitutional/legal right

questions.q: Under Article 300A, a person can be deprived of their property:
o: At the discretion of any government official with no legal authority required
Only by 'authority of law' — no deprivation is permitted without valid legal sanction
Only by a unanimous Parliamentary vote
questions.src: Constitution of India, Article 300A and Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat (Supreme Court, 1995) — 'if there is no law, there is no deprivation'

questions.q: In Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat (1995), the Supreme Court held that the right to property under Article 300A:
o: Is part of the Constitution's Basic Structure and enjoys heightened protection
Is NOT part of the Constitution's Basic Structure, meaning the legislature retains broad power to enact acquisition/land reform laws
Was restored as a Fundamental Right by this judgment
Cannot be regulated by any legislation whatsoever
questions.src: Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat (Supreme Court, 1995) — held Article 300A is not a basic-structure feature, distinguishing it from genuinely entrenched constitutional guarantees
